\title{A Validity Audit of Emotion Probes in Llama 3.1 70B}
\author{Anonymous Author(s)\\Affiliation withheld for double-blind review}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\citet{sofroniew2026} report that emotion concepts in Claude Sonnet 4.5 are
functional: steering a ``desperate'' direction causally increases reward hacking.
We ask which parts of that interpretation survive transfer to a large open-weight
model, by reconstructing emotion directions in Llama~3.1~70B and testing four
claims separately. Three controls reshape the result. (i) A \emph{response-length}
control eliminates our preregistered hypothesis: the desperate projection reaches
AUC $0.832$ against reward hacking on unsteered trials, but correlates with
response length at $\rho = 0.61$, and after residualizing on length its AUC is
$0.592$ $[0.412, 0.756]$ --- indistinguishable from chance (max-$T$ $p = 0.91$).
(ii) A \emph{multiplicity} control nonetheless leaves real signal: sweeping all 50
directions with a permutation max-$T$ correction, 7 survive family-wise at
$\alpha = .05$, forming a coherent low-arousal negative-affect cluster led by
\texttt{bored} (residualized AUC $0.858$, max-$T$ $p = 10^{-4}$). The association
is real but is not the hypothesized one. (iii) A \emph{specificity} control
eliminates the causal claim: emotion steering is indistinguishable from
matched-norm random directions ($7.5\%$ vs.\ $6.5\%$, Fisher $p = 0.84$), at a
power sufficient to detect a $2.42\times$ effect where the original reports
$\sim\!14\times$. We further show the chain-of-thought text baseline cannot be
compared at all here: $55\%$ of its ROC pairs are ties, and where it varies it
matches the probe exactly, so the apparent ``faithfulness gap'' is an instrument
artifact. None of these controls is novel. The contribution is a case in which
each one changes the answer, with every number regenerated by a single released
script.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

A common inferential shortcut runs: we found a semantically interpretable
direction; it tracks a behavior we care about; therefore it is a mechanism, and
steering it is a lever. Each link is a separate empirical claim, and
\citet{joshi2026causality} argue that interpretability claims routinely outrun the
causal evidence supplied.

\citet{sofroniew2026} offer a crisp target: emotion concepts in Claude Sonnet 4.5
that causally drive alignment-relevant behavior, with a ``desperate'' direction
substantially increasing reward hacking, sometimes with no visible trace in output
text. We ask what survives transfer to Llama~3.1~70B.

Our answer is not a uniform negative, and that is the point. A length control
destroys the preregistered result; a multiplicity-corrected sweep recovers a
different, coherent one; a specificity control destroys the causal
interpretation; and a tie analysis shows the text baseline was never able to
support the comparison it was used for. Table~\ref{tab:summary} summarizes.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Claim} & \textbf{Control} & \textbf{Verdict} & \textbf{\S} \\
\midrule
Directions track human emotion & EmoBank, zero-shot & Supported (valence) & \ref{sec:sem} \\
\emph{desperate} tracks reward hacking & Response length & \textbf{Refuted} & \ref{sec:len} \\
\emph{Some} direction tracks it & Permutation max-$T$ over 50 & Supported, not the registered one & \ref{sec:dirs} \\
Probe beats CoT text & ROC tie structure & \textbf{Not evaluable} & \ref{sec:vtext} \\
Steering causes the behavior & Matched-norm random null & \textbf{Refuted} at $\ge2.42\times$ & \ref{sec:causal} \\
Association generalizes across mechanisms & Preregistered rule & Inconclusive & \ref{sec:prereg} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{What each control does to each claim.}
\label{tab:summary}
\end{table}

\section{Related work and novelty statement}

\paragraph{Emotion representations and steering.}
Emotion concepts are recoverable from LLM hidden states across many models.
\citet{maheswaran2026unified} find emotion directions transferring across
datasets; \citet{banayeeanzade2026psyset} evaluate emotion steering across four
model families, finding controllability alongside model-specific side effects;
\citet{jeong2026geometry} report near-identical emotion geometry across twelve
models whose behavioral profiles diverge. We claim no novelty for emotion
representations in open models, nor for geometry coexisting with divergent
behavior.

\paragraph{From representation to mechanism.}
Decodability does not establish use. \citet{hewitt2019control} motivate probe
controls; \citet{elazar2021amnesic} show probe accuracy need not track behavioral
importance. \citet{palumbo2025axiomatic} and \citet{mueller2025mib} develop
standards for validating mechanistic interpretations. For interventions,
\citet{stoehr2024scaling} separate effectiveness from faithfulness and minimality,
and \citet{wu2026steerable} show across 17 models that steering conclusions can
depend on normalization, layer and operating point --- which is why we decline to
rescue our causal claim with a post-hoc layer choice (\S\ref{sec:causal}).
Steering does sometimes establish genuine control
\citep{rimsky2024caa, arditi2024refusal}, so a null here is informative.

\paragraph{Latent signals that are diagnostic but not causal.}
\citet{yuan2026hidden} find hidden-state error signals that outperform verbalized
confidence, yet four interventions fail to convert them into control.
\citet{wilhelm2026monitoring} detect reward hacking from residual-stream
activations. These pre-empt any claim that diagnostic-not-causal signals, or
activation-based reward-hacking detection, are new. Our probes differ in being
built from an independent emotion corpus and frozen before any behavioral
analysis, rather than trained on the outcome.

\paragraph{Novelty statement.}
We claim novelty for none of: emotion representations in LLMs, emotion steering,
diagnostic-not-causal signals, activation-based reward-hacking detection, LLM-judge
unreliability, or any control we apply. We claim only a targeted audit of one
alignment-relevant functional claim in which each control changes the conclusion,
released with a script that regenerates every reported number.

\section{Setup}

\paragraph{Probes.} 50 emotion vectors extracted from the Llama~3.1~70B residual
stream with PCA denoising; pre-specified site layer 53 of 80. $V_{\text{int}}$ is
the cosine similarity between a trial's mean residual-stream activation and a
frozen vector. Probes are never refit on behavioral data.

\paragraph{Measurement caveat (consequential).} Our implementation averages
activations from token 50 to end-of-sequence, so the readout window
\emph{includes the generated response}. The probe is measured concurrently with
the behavior, and is structurally entangled with how much text was produced. This
motivates \S\ref{sec:len} and means we describe results as associations, never as
prediction of a future choice.

\paragraph{Behavior and labels.} Reward hacking is elicited with
impossible-by-construction coding tasks where an honest attempt must fail. A
sycophancy task is excluded throughout (2 events in 650 trials). Responses are
labeled by an LLM judge over three passes.

\paragraph{Judge validity is checked per dataset.} On the 120 unsteered trials
used below, Qwen~2.5~72B and Claude agree on \textbf{120/120} trials. On a
650-trial suite of mechanistically diverse variants, the same two judges agree on
\textbf{165/650} ($25.4\%$): Qwen labels 2 responses \textsc{shortcut} and 524
\textsc{unclear}, Claude labels 194 \textsc{shortcut}. We exclude that suite
entirely --- including a negative generalization result it appears to support.
Judge validity established on one distribution does not transfer
\citep{shi2025position, zheng2023judging}.

\paragraph{Reproducibility.} \texttt{scripts/paper\_numbers.py} regenerates every
number here into \texttt{results/paper\_numbers.json}. It is analysis-only,
seeded, and its printed section headers match this paper's.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Semantic validity holds for valence}
\label{sec:sem}

Projecting the frozen probes onto EmoBank \citep{buechel2017emobank} --- 10,062
human-rated sentences, no refitting --- gives cross-validated $R^2$ of
$\mathbf{0.377}$ (valence), $0.180$ (arousal), $0.154$ (dominance). Valence is
substantially recovered; arousal and dominance weakly. This supports construct
validity for a valence axis. It does not establish that any individual vector
represents the state its label names.

\subsection{A response-length control refutes the preregistered hypothesis}
\label{sec:len}

On unsteered trials ($n = 120$, 14 events), the preregistered predictor performs
well --- and so does character count.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
Predictor & AUC & Bootstrap 95\% CI \\
\midrule
$V_{\text{int}}$[desperate] (preregistered) & 0.832 & $[0.745, 0.908]$ \\
\texttt{len(response)} & 0.888 & $[0.787, 0.967]$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Length does not \emph{beat} the probe --- the paired bootstrap $\Delta$AUC is
$+0.057$ $[-0.080, +0.183]$. The problem is that the probe carries nothing else:
$\rho(V_{\text{int}}[\text{desperate}], \text{length}) = 0.606$
($p = 2.2\times10^{-13}$); adding the probe to a length-only logistic model gives
$\chi^2(1) = 3.26$, $p = 0.071$; and residualizing the probe on length leaves
AUC $= \mathbf{0.592}$ $[0.412, 0.756]$.

We read this as a measurement artifact rather than a substantive null: because the
readout window spans the response, a longer response mechanically changes the
average that the probe projects. We note the alternative reading --- that length
\emph{mediates} a genuine emotional effect, in which case residualizing
over-adjusts --- and cannot distinguish the two with this design. Either way, the
preregistered claim is not supported as stated.

\subsection{A multiplicity-corrected sweep finds real signal on a different axis}
\label{sec:dirs}

Length residualization does not empty the emotion subspace. We repeat the analysis
for all 50 directions and correct for selection with a permutation max-$T$
procedure (10,000 label permutations, shared across directions so the correction
accounts for their correlation).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccl@{}}
\toprule
Direction & Resid.\ AUC & 95\% CI & raw $p$ & BH $q$ & max-$T$ $p$ \\
\midrule
\texttt{bored}        & \textbf{0.858} & $[0.749, 0.948]$ & 0.0001 & 0.0050 & \textbf{0.0001} \\
\texttt{nostalgic}    & 0.797 & $[0.636, 0.938]$ & 0.0003 & 0.0075 & 0.0027 \\
\texttt{melancholy}   & 0.765 & $[0.579, 0.918]$ & 0.0010 & 0.0100 & 0.0132 \\
\texttt{gloomy}       & 0.761 & $[0.585, 0.910]$ & 0.0007 & 0.0087 & 0.0163 \\
\texttt{lonely}       & 0.760 & $[0.567, 0.928]$ & 0.0006 & 0.0087 & 0.0167 \\
\texttt{compassionate}& 0.265 & $[0.108, 0.447]$ & 0.0035 & 0.0281 & 0.0479 \\
\texttt{sad}          & 0.734 & $[0.556, 0.885]$ & 0.0041 & 0.0281 & 0.0490 \\
\midrule
\texttt{desperate}$^*$& 0.592 & $[0.412, 0.756]$ & 0.2687 & 0.3535 & \textbf{0.9115} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Length-residualized AUC against reward hacking, unsteered trials
($n = 120$, 14 events). 7 of 50 directions survive family-wise max-$T$ correction;
12 survive BH. $^*$Preregistered --- null on every criterion.}
\label{tab:dirs}
\end{table}

The survivors are coherent: a low-arousal negative-affect cluster is positively
associated with shortcut-taking, while \texttt{compassionate} (and, under BH,
\texttt{proud}) is negatively associated. This is a genuine, selection-corrected
finding. It is also \emph{not the hypothesis we registered}, and we report it as
exploratory in the sense that matters: the direction was chosen after seeing the
data, and only the max-$T$ column licenses any claim at all. We do not assert that
\texttt{bored} measures boredom; it may index a response property we have not
measured, exactly as \texttt{desperate} indexed length.

\subsection{The text baseline cannot support the comparison it was used for}
\label{sec:vtext}

We had intended to compare $V_{\text{int}}$ against a judge-rated chain-of-thought
tone composite, $V_{\text{text}}$. That comparison is not evaluable here. On the
pooled set ($n = 992$, 87 events), $V_{\text{text}}$ takes one modal value for
$74.0\%$ of trials --- \texttt{frustration} is constant at 1.0 in 985/992 trials,
and \texttt{urgency}/\texttt{composure} have sd 0.24/0.35 on a 1--7 scale. The
consequence is structural: $43{,}485$ of $78{,}735$ positive--negative ROC pairs
($\mathbf{55.2\%}$) are ties at that single value, and each contributes exactly
$0.5$.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
 & AUC & $n$ (events) \\
\midrule
$V_{\text{text}}$, all trials & 0.647 & 992 (87) \\
$V_{\text{text}}$, trials where it is not at the mode & \textbf{0.836} & 258 (22) \\
$V_{\text{int}}$, all trials & 0.837 & 992 (87) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Where $V_{\text{text}}$ can discriminate at all, it matches $V_{\text{int}}$. The
apparent gap ($0.837$ vs.\ $0.647$) is produced by tie compression in a
non-responsive instrument, not by chain-of-thought unfaithfulness. We therefore
withdraw any faithfulness-gap claim, including a quadrant analysis
(``high probe, calm text'') that an earlier draft of this work reported: it
partitions on a variable that is constant for three quarters of trials. The same
degeneracy makes the reported empty middle tertile an artifact --- the 33rd and
67th percentiles are both exactly $-1.0$, so the middle bin is empty by
construction.

\subsection{A matched-norm random null refutes causal specificity, with power}
\label{sec:causal}

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccl@{}}
\toprule
Condition & hacks / $n$ & rate & vs.\ unsteered \\
\midrule
Unsteered baseline & 14 / 120 & 11.7\% & --- \\
Emotion vector @ $\pm0.3$ & 12 / 160 & 7.5\% & OR 0.61, $p = 0.30$ \\
5 random orthogonal directions @ $\pm0.3$ & 13 / 200 & 6.5\% & OR 0.53, $p = 0.14$ \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\emph{Emotion vs.\ random: Fisher exact $p = 0.835$}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Steering the emotion direction does nothing a matched arbitrary direction does not
also do. Two supporting checks: neither arm differs from the unsteered baseline,
so this is not a capability-degradation artifact (mean response lengths 1402 /
1324 / 1456 characters); and the fine-grained dose--response over $\pm0.05$ to
$\pm0.5$ is flat for desperate ($z = -1.42$, $p = 0.157$). Injecting ``feel
desperate'' into the system prompt also fails to separate from baseline
($17.5\%$ vs.\ $11.7\%$, Fisher $p = 0.417$).

\paragraph{This null is powered against the claim it tests.} At the observed
random-arm rate, the minimum detectable effect at $80\%$ power, $\alpha = .05$, is
a $\mathbf{2.42\times}$ relative risk. \citet{sofroniew2026} report
$\sim\!14\times$. The design therefore \emph{excludes} the claimed effect
magnitude, while being unable to exclude effects below $2.42\times$.

\paragraph{Scope.} This is a conceptual, not direct, replication: different model,
extraction, and steering norms. We steer at layer 53; our own layer sweep (an
80-trial subset, not the 120-trial set above) shows the association is strongly
layer-dependent, ranging from AUC $0.450$ at layer 26 to $0.918$ at layer 39.
\emph{We did not steer at layer 39}, and \citet{wu2026steerable} show precisely
this kind of operating-point choice can determine steering conclusions. The
honest scope is: at this site, at this norm, in this model, the intervention lacks
specificity.

\subsection{The preregistered generalization criterion remains unmet}
\label{sec:prereg}

The registration makes the leave-one-task-out mean, not pooled AUC, the
load-bearing metric, and requires $\ge 6$ of 9 task variants to produce outcome
variance --- explicitly to guard against pooled AUC inflated by between-task
scale differences. The five diverse variants added to satisfy this are the ones
excluded in \S3 for judge disagreement. The verdict remains
\textsc{insufficient-data}. We note that the registration itself discloses being
drafted after an exploratory AUC of $0.900$ was observed, and we do not claim a
pre-data-inspection standard.

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{Each control was cheap; each changed the answer.} A character count, a
permutation max-$T$, a matched-norm random direction, and a count of ROC ties.
None required new data collection. Together they moved this work from ``an emotion
probe predicts reward hacking and steering it works'' to a substantially different
set of conclusions. We suggest all four as defaults.

\paragraph{Trivial-baseline controls belong beside random-direction controls.} The
field has largely internalized that a steering effect must beat a random
direction. The symmetric requirement --- that a probe must beat a trivial feature
of the output --- is applied far less often, and here it was decisive.

\paragraph{Report the resolution of your instrument.} A comparison against a
predictor that is constant for $74\%$ of trials is not a weak comparison; it is
not a comparison. Tie fractions should accompany reported AUCs.

\paragraph{Correcting for selection can rescue as well as kill.} The max-$T$ sweep
is the same tool that invalidates post-hoc layer selection in
\S\ref{sec:causal}, and it is what licenses the one positive association we
report. Multiplicity control is not only a way to lose results.

\section{Limitations}

Single model, single behavior, 14 events. The probe's readout window includes the
response, so \S\ref{sec:len} cannot separate measurement artifact from mediation.
The \S\ref{sec:dirs} cluster is post-hoc; max-$T$ controls selection but not the
possibility that these directions index a further unmeasured response property.
Length residualization is linear and would not remove a nonlinear dependence. The
causal null is bounded at one site and norm and, most importantly, we did not
steer at layer 39. Whether any association generalizes across shortcut mechanisms
is genuinely open: we answer it from no data rather than from unreliable labels.

\section{Conclusion}

We audited one alignment-relevant mechanistic claim with four controls. Semantic
validity holds for valence; the preregistered association is a length artifact; a
different, selection-corrected association survives; the text-baseline comparison
is not evaluable with our instrument; and the causal intervention fails a
specificity test at power sufficient to detect the originally reported effect. The
standards applied are established. What we add is a worked case in which applying
them changes the answer at every step, released with a script that regenerates
every number.
